title: Soft White Bread (Tangzhong Method)
description: A soft, pale, everyday loaf that stays tender for days without milk, butter, or yellowing — thanks to the tangzhong technique. Note: tangzhong water has been increased to account for evaporation.

ingredients.item: water (accounts for evaporation during cooking tangzhong)

method.instruction: Make the tangzhong: In a small saucepan, combine 30g flour and 190g water. Cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it thickens into a paste (around 65°C). Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature.
In a large bowl, combine the 560g flour, salt, sugar, yeast, and bread improver (if using).
Add the cooled tangzhong, 180g water, and oil to the dry ingredients.
Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead for 10-12 minutes by hand (or 7-8 minutes in a stand mixer) until smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky but not sticky.
Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp tea towel, and let rise in a warm place for 1-1.5 hours until doubled in size.
Punch down the dough and shape into a loaf. Place in a greased loaf tin (approximately 20cm x 10cm).
Cover and let rise for another 45-60 minutes until the dough has risen about 1-2cm above the rim of the tin.
Bake for 28-32 minutes until the top is golden brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom.
Remove from tin immediately and cool on a wire rack for at least 30 minutes before slicing.

notes.title: Why Tangzhong Works
notes.content: The tangzhong (water roux) pre-gelatinizes the starch, allowing the dough to hold more moisture. This keeps the bread soft and fresh for 2-3 days without refrigeration.

notes.title: Neutral Oil for Pale Crumb
notes.content: Using neutral oil instead of butter keeps the crumb pale white. The tangzhong locks in moisture without making the dough sticky.

notes.title: Weighing Tangzhong
notes.content: For best results, weigh your tangzhong after cooking to ensure hydration is correct. It should weigh approximately 150-160g after cooking.
